problems.title: Strict order from a partial order
problems.statement:
Suppose that $S$ is a set and $\preceq$ is a relation on $S$ with the following properties:

- For all $x \in S$, $x \preceq x$.
- For all $x, y \in S$, if $x \preceq y$ and $y \preceq x$ then $x = y$.
- For all $x, y, z \in S$, if $x \preceq y$ and $y \preceq z$, then $x \preceq z$.

Define a new relation $\prec$ on $S$ by $x \prec y$ iff $x \preceq y$ and $x \ne y$. Does this define an order conforming to Definition 1.5 in Rudin? If so, prove it; if not, exhibit a counterexample.

problems.title: Lexicographic order on $\mathbb{C}$

problems.title: Archimedean property of $\mathbb{Q}$

problems.title: Proofs by induction
problems.statement:
Review the logic of a proof by induction. (The – not always reliable – wikipedia gives a good explanation in this case.)

(a) Prove that $(1 + 2 + \cdots + n)^2 = 1^3 + 2^3 + \cdots + n^3$ for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

(b) Find a proof of the Bernoulli inequality:

$$
(1 + x)^n \ge 1 + nx \qquad \text{for all } x \in \mathbb{R}, x \ge -1 \text{ and } n \in \mathbb{N}, n \ge 2.
$$

(not for credit) Show that strict inequality $(1 + x)^n > 1 + nx$ holds unless $x = 0$.

problems.title: Product of compact sets in $\mathbb{R}^2$
problems.statement:
Let $E$ and $F$ be two compact subsets of the real numbers $\mathbb{R}$ with the standard (Euclidian) metric $d(x, y) = \lvert x - y \rvert$. Show that the Cartesian product

$$
E \times F = \{(x, y) \mid x \in E \text{ and } y \in F\}
$$

is a compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the metric $d_2(\vec{u}, \vec{v}) = \lVert \vec{u} - \vec{v} \rVert_2$. (Recall that the norm $\lVert \cdot \rVert_2$ is defined by $\lVert (x, y) \rVert_2 = (x^2 + y^2)^{1/2}$.)

problems.title: The common-ancestor relation
problems.statement: Let $H$ be the set of all human beings (past and present). Let $R$ be the usual family relation on $H$; that is, for $h, k \in H$ we have $(h, k) \in R$ if and only if $h$ and $k$ have a common ancestor. Show that $R$ is reflexive and symmetric, but not transitive.

problems.title: Reciprocals of Cauchy sequences in $\mathbb{Q}$
problems.statement:
(a) Let $(a_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb{Q}$, such that $a_n$ does *not* converge to $0$. Show that there is an $\omega > 0$ and an $N \in \mathbb{N}$ so that $\lvert a_n \rvert > \omega$ for all $n \ge N$. Moreover, show that the sign of $a_n$ is constant for large $n$.

(b) Following part **(a)**, show that if $(a_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb{Q}$ that does not converge to $0$, then $(1/a_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb{Q}$. [*Remark*: it would be tempting to solve this problem by noting that, thinking of $(a_n)$ living in the bigger complete metric space $\mathbb{R}$, we can replace the word "Cauchy" by "convergent", which makes for an easy proof. That is *not* the intention of the problem; you should work directly within $\mathbb{Q}$.]

problems.title: Lecture $\liminf$ agrees with Rudin's $s_*$
problems.statement:
Let $(s_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}$. Show that the definition of $\liminf$ in the lecture coincides with the $s_*$ of Rudin 3.16. In the lecture, we defined

$$
\liminf_{n \to \infty} s_n := \begin{cases} \lim_{n \to \infty} \inf\{s_k \mid k \ge n\} & \text{; if limit of infima exists,} \\ -\infty & \text{; if } (s_n) \text{ is not bounded below;} \\ \infty & \text{; if } s_n \to \infty. \end{cases}
$$

problems.title: Subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ up to finite difference
problems.statement:
Let $\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{N})$ denote the set of all subsets of $\mathbb{N}$. Define a relation $\mathscr{D}$ on $\mathscr{P}(\mathbb{N})$ as follows: $(A, B) \in \mathscr{D}$ if the symmetric difference

$$
A \Delta B := (A \cup B) \setminus (A \cap B)
$$

is finite. (That is: $A$ and $B$ only differ by finitely many numbers.)

(a) Show that $\mathscr{D}$ is an equivalence relation.

(b) Show that all finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ are in the same equivalence class of $\mathscr{D}$.

(c) Show that each equivalence class of $\mathscr{D}$ is a *countable* family of subsets. [*Hint*: fix any subset $A_0 \in \mathscr{P}(\mathbb{N})$, and for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$ consider the classes $A_0^{(n)} = \{A \subseteq \mathbb{N} \,;\, A \text{ differs from } A_0 \text{ by } n \text{ numbers}\}$. Show that $A_0^{(n)}$ is countable, and that the equivalence class $[A_0]_{\mathscr{D}}$ is the union of the countably-many $A_0^{(n)}$.]

**not for credit:** Conclude that there are uncountably many equivalences classes of $\mathscr{D}$.

problems.title: Cauchy–Schwarz and the space $\ell^2$
problems.statement:
(a) Let $N \ge 1$ and let $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_N$ and $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_N$ be real numbers. Verify that

$$
\left( \sum_{i=1}^N a_i b_i \right)^2 + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^N (a_i b_j - a_j b_i)^2 = \left( \sum_{i=1}^N a_i^2 \right) \left( \sum_{j=1}^N b_j^2 \right)
$$

and conclude the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality

$$
\left\lvert \sum_{i=1}^N a_i b_i \right\rvert \le \left( \sum_{i=1}^N a_i^2 \right)^{1/2} \left( \sum_{j=1}^N b_j^2 \right)^{1/2}.
$$

Then use the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality inequality to prove the triangle inequality

$$
\left( \sum_{i=1}^N (a_i + b_i)^2 \right)^{1/2} \le \left( \sum_{i=1}^N a_i^2 \right)^{1/2} + \left( \sum_{j=1}^N b_j^2 \right)^{1/2}.
$$

(Hint: square both sides.)

(b) Let now

$$
X = \left\{ a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R} \;\middle\vert\; \textstyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a(n)^2 \text{ converges} \right\} = \left\{ (a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset \mathbb{R} \;\middle\vert\; \textstyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^2 < \infty \right\}
$$

and define a norm and induced metric

$$
\lVert (a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \rVert_2 = \left( \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n^2 \right)^{1/2}, \qquad d_2((a_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}, (b_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}) = \lVert (a_n - b_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \rVert_2.
$$

Use part a) to show that $(X, d_2)$ is a metric space. (Hint: One way to solve this is to first prove that $(X, \lVert \cdot \rVert_2)$ is a normed vector space.)

problems.title: Banach fixed-point theorem
problems.statement:
**Banach fixed-point theorem:** Let $(X, d)$ be a complete metric space. Suppose $f : X \to X$ has the property that, for some number $c \in (0, 1)$,

$$
d(f(x), f(y)) \le c \cdot d(x, y) \quad \text{for all} \quad x, y \in X.
$$

(a) Suppose $y_n \in X$ is any convergent sequence, with limit $y$. Prove that $f(y_n)$ is a convergent sequence, and $f(y_n) \to f(y)$.

(b) Fix any point $x_0 \in X$, and iteratively define $x_{n+1} = f(x_n)$ for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Show that

$$
\sum_{j=0}^\infty d(x_{j+1}, x_j)
$$

is a convergent series. [*Hint*: it is bounded above by a geometric series.]

(c) Show that the sequence $(x_n)$ of iterates of $f$ starting at $x_0$, as above, is a Cauchy sequence. Conclude that it converges to some point $x_\infty \in X$. [*Hint*: Let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, and suppose $m \ge n$. Then $m = n + k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Show that $d(x_m, x_n) \le c^n \cdot d(x_k, x_0)$, and $d(x_k, x_0) \le d(x_k, x_{k-1}) + d(x_{k-1}, x_{k-2}) + \cdots + d(x_1, x_0) \le \sum_{j=0}^\infty d(x_{j+1}, x_j)$. Conclude that $d(x_m, x_n) \to 0$ as $m, n \to \infty$.]

(d) Show that, given any starting point $x_0$, the limit $x_\infty$ of the sequence of iterates in **(c)** is a *fixed-point* of $f$: i.e. $f(x_\infty) = x_\infty$. [*Hint*: using part **(a)**, compare $d(f(x_\infty), x_\infty)$ to $d(f(x_n), x_n)$.]

(e) Let $x_0, y_0$ be any two points in $X$. Let $x_{n+1} = f(x_n)$ and $y_{n+1} = f(y_n)$ be the sequences of iterates. Show that $d(x_n, y_n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. Conclude that $x_\infty = y_\infty$, and that $f$ has a *unique* fixed point.

problems.title: Maps to and from a discrete metric space
problems.statement:
Let $(S, d_S)$ be a set equipped with the discrete metric (i.e. $d_S(t, r) = 1$ for $t \ne r$).

(a) Show that any map $f : S \to X$ into another metric space $X$ is continuous; using the definition of continuity by sequences.

(b) Show that any map $f : S \to X$ into another metric space $X$ is continuous; using the definition of continuity by $\epsilon$- and $\delta$-balls.

(c) Which maps $f : \mathbb{R} \to S$ are continuous? (Give an easy characterization and prove it.)

problems.title: A step function on $\mathbb{Q}$ at $\sqrt{2}$
problems.statement:
Consider the function $h : \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{R}$ given by

$$
h(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & ; x^2 < 2, \\ 1 & ; x^2 > 2. \end{cases}
$$

(a) Is $h$ continuous?

(b) Can $h$ be continuously extended to $\tilde{h} : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$? (I.e. such that $\tilde{h}(x) = h(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{Q}$.)

problems.title: Continuity of the complex exponential
problems.statement:
Prove that the function $f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$, $z \mapsto e^z = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1}{n!} z^n$ is continuous by following the steps below.

(a) Fix $T > 0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. Show that there exists an $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that

$$
\sum_{n=N}^\infty \frac{t^n}{n!} < \varepsilon \qquad \forall t \in [0, T].
$$

[*Hint*: The series for $e^T$ converges.]

(b) Show continuity at $z \in \mathbb{C}$ by splitting

$$
e^z - e^x = \sum_{n=1}^{N-1} \frac{1}{n!}(z^n - x^n) + \sum_{n=N}^\infty \frac{1}{n!} z^n - \sum_{n=N}^\infty \frac{1}{n!} x^n.
$$

[*Hint*: First use (a) with $T = \lvert z \rvert + 1$, then use the fact that polynomials are continuous.]

problems.title: One-sided limits in $\epsilon$-$\delta$ form
problems.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to Y$ be a map to a metric space $Y$. Show that, for $a \in \mathbb{R}$ and $y \in Y$, the statement $f(a+) = y$ is equivalent to the following:

$$
\forall \epsilon > 0 \ \exists \delta > 0 \ \forall x \in (a, a + \delta) : d(f(x), y) < \epsilon.
$$

Formulate the analogous statement in the case of the left limit $f(a-) = y$.

problems.title: Uniform continuity and Cauchy sequences
problems.statement:
(a) Let $f : X \to Y$ be a uniformly continuous function between metric spaces. Show that if $(x_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ is a Cauchy sequence in $X$, then $(f(x_n))_{n=1}^\infty$ is a Cauchy sequence in $Y$. Show, therefore, that the function $f(x) = 1/x^2$ defined on $(0, \infty)$ is not uniformly continuous.

(b) Problem 6, page 99 in Rudin (You may assume that $f$ is a real valued function on $E \subset \mathbb{R}$. This result does hold in general also with the metric $d((x, y), (x', y')) = d_X(x, x') + d_Y(y, y')$ on the product $X \times Y$ of two metric spaces $(X, d_X)$ and $(Y, d_Y)$. Hint: One direction is a little subtle. Try e.g. a proof by contradiction to the $\epsilon, \delta$-definition of continuity, and use sequential compactness.)

problems.title: A metric on power series and evaluation maps
problems.statement:
Let $P$ denote the space of power series with radius of convergence $R > 1$:

$$
P = \left\{ \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n z^n \,;\, a_n \in \mathbb{C}, \limsup_{n \to \infty} \lvert a_n \rvert^{1/n} < 1 \right\}.
$$

(a) Define $d : P \times P \to \mathbb{R}$ as follows: If $p(z) = \sum_n a_n z^n$ and $q(z) = \sum_n b_n z^n$, then

$$
d(p, q) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \lvert a_n - b_n \rvert.
$$

Show that $d$ is a metric on $P$. [*Hint*: You can use your knowledge of $\ell^1$.]

(b) Fix $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}$ with $\lvert z_0 \rvert \le 1$. Show that the *evaluation map* $\mathrm{ev}_{z_0}(p) = p(z_0)$ for $p \in P$ is a *uniformly continuous* function $P \to \mathbb{C}$ (in terms of the metric $d$ from part **(a)** on $P$, and the usual Euclidean metric on $\mathbb{C}$). [*Hint*: Try first with $z_0 = 1$.]

problems.title: The modulus $\delta_f(x, \epsilon)$ and uniform continuity
problems.statement:
Let $(X, d_X)$ and $(Y, d_Y)$ be metric spaces. For any continuous map $f : X \to Y$ define a function $\delta_f : X \times (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty) \cup \{\infty\}$ as follows:

$$
\delta_f(x, \epsilon) = \sup\{\delta > 0 \mid \forall t \in X \ d_X(x, t) < \delta \Rightarrow d_Y(f(x), f(t)) < \epsilon\}.
$$

Note that this supremum may be $\infty$ if the continuity condition holds for all $\delta > 0$; e.g. for $f$ constant. In the following, we use the definition of order $<$ and infimum in the extended reals.

(a) Show that the statement "$f$ is continuous at $x$" is equivalent to "$\delta_f(x, \epsilon) > 0$ for each $\epsilon > 0$".

(b) Show that $f$ is uniformly continuous on $X$ iff $\inf_{x \in X} \delta_f(x, \epsilon) > 0$.

(c) Consider the function $f(x) = x^2$ defined on the metric space $X = [0, \infty)$. Show that for each $x \in X$

$$
\sup_{t \in X, d_X(x, t) < \delta} \lvert f(x) - f(t) \rvert = 2x\delta + \delta^2.
$$

(d) Use part **(c)** to show that $\delta_f(x, \epsilon) = \sqrt{x^2 + \epsilon} - x$. Show that, for fixed $\epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{x \to \infty}[\sqrt{x^2 + \epsilon} - x] = 0$. Conclude that $f$ is *not* uniformly continuous on $X$. [*Hint*: you can use Calculus here, but you needn't. Set $\varphi(x) = \sqrt{x^2 + \epsilon} - x$. Show that $\varphi(x) \ge 0$, and that $\varphi(x)^2 + 2x\,\varphi(x) = \epsilon$ for every $x$. Hence $0 \le \varphi(x) \le \epsilon/2x$.]

problems.title: Integrability of spikes at $1/n$
problems.statement:
Consider the following two real-valued functions on $[0, 1]$.

$$
f(x) = \begin{cases} 1, & x = \frac{1}{n} \text{ for some } n \in \mathbb{N} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \qquad g(x) = \begin{cases} n, & x = \frac{1}{n} \text{ for some } n \in \mathbb{N} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}.
$$

Show (from the definition) that $f \in \mathscr{R}$ (i.e. $f$ is Riemann-integrable), with $\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx = 0$, but $g \notin \mathscr{R}$.

problems.title: Sets of measure zero
problems.statement:
A subset $N \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is said to have *measure* $0$ if, for each $\epsilon > 0$, there is a sequence (finite or countable) of balls $(B_n)$ with radii $r_n$ so that $N \subseteq \bigcup_n B_n$ and $\sum_n r_n < \epsilon$.

(a) Let $N$ be a set of measure $0$ in $\mathbb{R}$. Prove that the complement $N^c$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$.

(b) Show (from the definition) that the only open set that has measure $0$ is $\varnothing$.

(c) Can measure $0$ sets be closed? Non-compact? Dense?

problems.title: The $L^1$ distance on $\mathscr{R}^1[a, b]$
problems.statement:
Let $\mathscr{R}^1[a, b]$ denote the set of all functions $f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ with the property that $\lvert f \rvert$ is Riemann integrable. Define a function $d_1 : \mathscr{R}^1[a, b] \times \mathscr{R}^1[a, b] \to \mathbb{R}_+$ by

$$
d_1(f, g) = \int_a^b \lvert f - g \rvert.
$$

(a) Show that if $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$, then $f \in \mathscr{R}^1[a, b]$.

(b) Is the converse of (a) true? [*Hint*: think about the function $g$ that equals $1$ on $\mathbb{Q}$ and $0$ on $\mathbb{Q}^c$; find non-zero constants $a, b$ so that $\lvert ag + b \rvert$ is constant.]

(c) Prove that $d_1$ satisfies all the axioms of a metric on $\mathscr{R}^1[a, b]$ except that $d_1(f, g) = 0$ for some $f \ne g$.

(d) Assume that $f, g$ are continuous on $[a, b]$. Prove that $d_1(f, g) = 0$ iff $f = g$ on $[a, b]$. Conclude that the subset $\mathscr{C}[a, b]$ of continuous functions in $\mathscr{R}^1[a, b]$ is a metric space under the metric $d_1$.

problems.title: $(\mathscr{C}[-1, 1], d_1)$ is not complete
problems.statement:
Consider the metric space $(\mathscr{C}[-1, 1], d_1)$ from **4(d)** (here $a = -1, b = 1$).

(a) Let $f_n$ denote the function

$$
f_n(x) = \begin{cases} 1, & x > \frac{1}{n}, \\ nx, & 0 \le x \le \frac{1}{n}, \\ 0, & x < 0 \end{cases}.
$$

Show that $f_n \in \mathscr{C}[-1, 1]$, and calculate $\int_0^1 f_n$.

(b) Show that the sequence $(f_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in terms of the metric $d_1$.

(c) Does $f_n$ converge in $\mathscr{C}[-1, 1]$? Is this metric space complete?

problems.title: Convergence of improper integrals
problems.statement:
Use the definitions in Problems 7 and 8 of *Rudin* to answer the following questions:

(a) For which $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ does the integral

$$
\int_0^1 \frac{\sin t}{t^\alpha}\,dt

converge (absolutely)? (*Hint*: First try to understand the convergence of the integral of $\frac{1}{t^\gamma}$ on the interval $[0, 1]$).

(b) For which $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$ does the integral

$$
\int_1^\infty \frac{e^{-t}}{t^\beta}\,dt
$$

converge (absolutely)? (*Hint*: First try to understand the convergence of the integral of $\frac{1}{t^\gamma}$ on the interval $[1, \infty)$).

problems.title: Uniform convergence of Taylor polynomials
problems.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a smooth function (i.e. all derivatives exist) and fix $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}$. The Taylor series $T(x)$ of $f$ at $x_0$ is defined as the pointwise limit $T(x) = \lim_{k \to \infty} P_k(x)$ of the Taylor polynomials

$$
P_k(x) = \sum_{n=0}^k \frac{f^{(n)}(x_0)}{n!} (x - x_0)^n.
$$

(a) For which $r > 0$ do the Taylor polynomials $P_k$ converge uniformly on $B_r(x_0)$ to $T$? (Hint: Write $T(x)$ as a series and compare $r$ with its radius of convergence. You can use e.g. Rudin Theorem 7.10.)

(b) Recall Taylor's error formula for $\lvert f(x) - P_k(x) \rvert$. Deduce that $f = T$ on the ball $B_A(x_0)$ if $A > 0$ satisfies

$$
A < \lim_{n \to \infty} \left( \frac{1}{n!} \sup_{z \in B_A(x_0)} \lvert f^{(n)}(z) \rvert \right)^{-1/n}.
$$
